source.notes: Synthetic writing authored against the frozen rhythm-and-repetition definitions and the existing hedge-stacking definition where assessed. Reviews and measured results are stored separately.

instructions: Protected holdout: keep writing, labels, snippets and individual judgments outside prompt authoring. Model evaluation requires separate user authorization.

A sample allows a researcher to study part of a population.
Choosing the sample requires deciding who can participate.
The sample may contain people from several towns, and the sample size affects the precision of an estimate.
After collecting responses from the sample, researchers describe the sample in their methods section.
A text can reveal how a dispute was presented to contemporary readers.
Historians examine the text alongside letters and newspaper reports.
Dating the text helps establish its audience, while comparing copies of the text reveals revisions.
The text may survive in several editions, each preserving part of the text's publication history.
The group met once a week during the study.
Researchers asked the group to discuss local transport, then recorded how the group reached decisions.
Membership of the group remained stable for six months.
At the final session, the group reviewed a summary, and each person could correct the group's recorded comments.
A score summarizes performance on the memory task.
Researchers calculate the score from the number of correct responses.
A higher score indicates better recall, but the score can also depend on fatigue.
Before interpreting the score, the analyst checks the testing conditions and compares the score with the participant's earlier result.
A source provides evidence for a historical claim.
To assess the source, students identify its author and intended audience.
They then place the source in its political setting.
Comparing the source with other documents can reveal omissions.
A reliable interpretation explains what the source contributes and how the source was preserved.
The trial tested a reading intervention in four schools.
During the trial, teachers used the new materials twice a week.
Researchers visited each school before the trial ended and collected attendance records.
Results from the trial appeared in a departmental report, where the trial methods were described alongside the trial outcomes.
Images can provide evidence about clothing and social rank.
Students examine each image for details that identify its setting.
Dating the images requires comparing the images with other surviving examples.
A caption may explain who commissioned an image, but the images themselves can suggest additional questions about the scenes.
A rule describes which moves are permitted in the game.
Players learn the rule by observing examples, then apply the rule to unfamiliar positions.
The rule may be expressed verbally or demonstrated with pieces.
Researchers ask participants to explain the rule after playing, revealing how accurately they understood the rule.

Check that the stamp keeps its original dimensions.
If the stamp appears stretched, clear the saved aspect ratio before using the stamp on a document.
Empty the bottom drawer before the movers arrive.
Photograph the drawer contents, then put the photograph inside the drawer.
Tape the drawer shut using the removable tape from reception.
Write your room number on the drawer so facilities can return it.
Keep the drawer key with you rather than in the packing crate.
Take the unopened roll to the cutting table.
Check the roll against the dye-lot slip before removing the wrapper.
Measure the roll from the marked end, then photograph the roll beside the tape.
Return the roll to rack B if the shade differs.
Mark that roll as awaiting approval so nobody cuts it.
Print the label before unplugging the old monitor.
Attach the label to the cable at the monitor end.
Copy the label onto the docking station sheet, then photograph the label in place.
If the label smears, print another before moving anything.
Leave the label visible when packing so the installer can match connections.
Take one empty crate from the store before picking apples.
Write your plot number on the crate.
Fill the crate only to the painted line so volunteers can lift it.
Leave the crate under the awning, then record the crate on the weighing sheet.
Collect your crate after the juice has been bottled.
Collect a token from reception before joining the pottery queue.
Keep the token until your number is called.
Give the token to the instructor when you enter, then collect a new token if you want a second session.
A token reserves one stool, so each child needs a separate token even when sharing clay.
Bring a clean jar to the seed exchange.
Label the jar with the variety and harvest year.
Keep the jar open while a volunteer checks the seeds for moisture.
Close the jar after inspection and place the jar on the numbered shelf.
Take an empty jar home if you need one for next season.
The dishwasher basket is removable, which matters in my narrow kitchen.
I lift the basket onto the counter before loading forks, carry the basket back by its handle, and clip the basket into the rack.
Leaving the basket loose causes rattling.
Securing the basket solved that noise throughout a week of washes.
Changing the blade takes longer than the advert suggests.
I loosen the blade with the supplied tool, wrap the blade in cardboard, and remove the blade without touching its edge.
The replacement blade fits only one way round.
Once I tighten the blade, the cutter works cleanly, but I would prefer a quicker clamp.
Here, a case means one household, not one respondent.
A case may therefore contain several interviews.
We assign each case a number and store individual responses beneath it.
Counting a case once estimates household prevalence.
Counting every interview within a case would give larger households more influence simply because more people answered.
A case with no completed interviews remains in the recruitment log.
Number the slide before adding the specimen.
Put one drop in the centre of the slide, then lower the coverslip at an angle.
Place the slide on the microscope stage with the number facing upward.
Focus at low power before moving the slide.
Return the slide to its numbered rack after recording your observations.
Keep the numbered slide until the tutor has checked your sketch.
Mark the top of the sediment core immediately after extraction.
Photograph the core before splitting it.
Cut the core lengthwise, then reserve half the core for storage.
Sample the exposed half of the core at the numbered depths.
Keep the core upright during transfer so loose surface material does not move into older layers.
At our repair cafe, I attach a ticket before opening an appliance.
The ticket records the owner's description, then stays beside the parts tray.
Another volunteer signs the ticket after testing.
We give the ticket back with the appliance and photograph the ticket for our records.
A missing ticket pauses a return until ownership is confirmed.
Her grandfather had taught her to inspect a knot in three places.
She found the knot at the cleat, pressed the knot to feel for slack, then traced the knot back to its standing end.
Only after checking that the knot held under tension did she trust the knot with her weight over the water.
